Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty Images Trump administration UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’ Edward Helmore Sun 27 Sep 2026 12.28 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Trump administration ’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran ’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”. Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz. “They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said. Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”. Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz Read more In comments to Axios on Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.” Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace. Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”. Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel. “Our conditions are clear, ​and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.” Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal. “We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.” The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for ​talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not ​accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will ​defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines US Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region. Senate Republicans block Democratic effort to end US war with Iran Read more Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz. “I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.” Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”. “They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.” Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating. “The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.” Explore more on these topics Trump administration US-Israel war on Iran US politics Iran Middle East and north Africa Donald Trump United Nations news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Lithuania says it supports an initiative by several EU countries but does not currently plan to join it. The ministers meeting in Luxembourg were also expected to give final approval to new EU rules that would expand authoritiesâ powers to detain people facing removal and allow the creation of so-called return centres outside the bloc. The initiative is being promoted by a group of five countries: Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands. Rwanda and Uganda are among the main candidates to host such centres. The centres could serve as destinations or transit points for people being removed from the EU, including those whose asylum applications have been rejected. Supporters say they could facilitate repatriation and deter people from attempting to enter the EU irregularly. Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas, who represented Lithuania at the meeting, said Lithuania did not face a large enough migration problem to participate in the initiative at present. Martynas Katelynas | P. Peleckis / BNS âLithuania does not have a problem of such a scale that we need to participate in this format, but we support the efforts of other European countries to solve this issue,â Katelynas told LRT. âIf there is a need, we will certainly support the initiative. And if at some point in the future we need it ourselves, we would certainly join.â Katelynas said EU countries currently implement only about one-third of decisions ordering migrants to be deported. He said irregular migration at Lithuaniaâs external border was currently under control, although the country had faced an increase in secondary migration earlier this summer. âThere are currently about 200 irregular migrants at Lithuaniaâs Foreigners Registration Centre, most of whom should be returned to Latvia or other Schengen countries,â Katelynas said. Foreigners' Registration Centre in PabradÄ | B. GerdÅ¾iÅ«nas / LRT The proposal for return centres has drawn criticism from human rights advocates and some politicians. European Parliament members Anna Strolenberg and Tineke Strik of the Greens group held an online news conference Wednesday following a visit to Uganda and Rwanda. They questioned whether the two countries were appropriate locations for EU return centres, citing concerns about human rights, conditions in the proposed facilities and their potential impact on local communities. They also argued that the centres would not address the causes of irregular migration and could become costly. EU ministers in Luxembourg were also due to discuss proposed changes to asylum rules that would apply during emergency situations, including circumstances in which migration is considered to be used as a tool of political pressure. Migrants in Ceuta | AP The debate follows a reported surge of migrants at Spainâs North African enclave of Ceuta this summer, when about 80,000 people were reported to have attempted to enter the territory. Some right-wing politicians and EU countries have argued that the right to seek asylum should be restricted in situations where migration is considered to be âinstrumentalisedâ. Swedish and Estonian ministers also arrived in Luxembourg seeking details from the European Commission on possible restrictions on Schengen visas for Russian citizens. Lithuania supports that initiative as well. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. Thanks for subscribing! https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/09/trum.text: US President Donald Trump declared the US has won the war with Iran and that renewed fighting was "highly unlikely," as US forces struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.“We won in Iran,” Trump said on Sunday. “It’s just a matter of closing it out now.”Trump also said that Iran was collapsing financially and militarily, adding that the US had three aircraft carriers in the region and had identified infrastructure targets including power plants and bridges."They're a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation," Trump claimed. "They're withering away financially. We've hit them militarily. We could finish them off."Iran's official figures put inflation at nearly 90% year-on-year in September.The US president further warned that his final decision on possible strikes "depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement."“We have 38 bridges in our sight that we can knock down in literally one hour,” he said, adding he was reluctant to act. “I don’t like ripping down bridges,” he said, adding that rebuilding Iran’s infrastructure could take a decade."I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don't know how hard I hit them," he said.Trump said the US had suffered no fatalities in the war. “Again, we haven’t lost anybody. No soldiers,” he said.The Pentagon’s official count puts the death toll at 23 service members killed since the war began in late February.Another Qeshm strike reportedExplosions were reported in Mahshahr, Qeshm, Sirik and Bandar Abbas on Sunday evening. Iran’s Tasnim news agency confirmed a US projectile struck Qeshm Island, saying no other areas in Hormozgan province were hit.It said sounds heard in Bandar Abbas and Sirik were related to Iranian security operations in the Strait of Hormuz.Earlier, Iran’s navy announced an oil tanker had struck a naval mine while crossing the strait and caught fire, saying the vessel was sailing on what it called a prohibited route.Iran labels ships transiting the strait's southern route under US naval guidance as violating its rules.On Saturday, CENTCOM reported an attack on a commercial ship in the Gulf of Oman, saying it had repeatedly attempted to breach the US naval blockade against Iran.Iran’s IRGC said two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines while crossing the strait.CENTCOM announced on Saturday the creation of a new task force, saying it would “support the ongoing efforts of the US government to prevent Iran from using land routes to transfer advanced weapons and other items.”Trump subsequently said the force was operating at full capacity alongside what he described as the largest naval blockade in history.Iran blasts Rubio's ‘ridiculous’ commentUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran’s demands were not only unacceptable but in some cases “overblown, ridiculous and really unrealistic.”He said he could report no progress in talks, that steps taken so far had not been very constructive, and that US actions in the Strait of Hormuz were defensive."I wouldn't say we're on the verge of a breakthrough. Trump would always prefer to solve every problem diplomatically. Sometimes that's not possible," Rubio said."But if there's a chance to do it, we will explore it. Right now, it hasn't been very productive."Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday rejected Rubio’s characterisation, saying that "pursuing the rights and interests of the Iranian nation was not unreasonable."He said Washington must end sanctions, the naval blockade and the war on all fronts before any negotiations could begin, and that Iran’s two-day proposal to restore security to the strait remained on the table.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the Democratic victory in the US midterm elections had paused the mediation process, with intermediaries not travelling for several days while the political situation settled.He wrote on X that the US must now choose between accepting Iran’s conditions or resuming the war, and that Tehran’s two-day proposal remained open."Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars," Araghchi said on X. "They had enough. So has our region."Qatar said Trump spoke by phone with Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss reducing regional tensions. The White House said Trump would meet Qatar’s Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House.Araghchi said he had been in contact in recent days with counterparts in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, Pakistan, Kuwait, Jordan, Turkey, Cyprus and Qatar.Trump told CBS in a separate interview that Iran was close to reaching an agreement but that the midterm result had given Tehran some hope. He said he was not looking to intensify the war and saw no reason to do so.Trump also said the US had an undisclosed Iranian underground facility under surveillance and could strike it within an hour if needed, but said this was not currently necessary.
